documents.title: AJCC cancer staging manual oral cavity 8th edition

chunks.content: Introduction Prostate cancer (PCa) represents a significant global health burden and is among the most prevalent cancers in men. The incidence of PCa has shown a consistent upward trend, driven by factors such as population aging, alongside changes in lifestyle and dietary patterns [ ]. For men with localized PCa treated with radical prostatectomy (RP), lymph node metastasis (LNM) is a paramount prognostic factor for recurrence and mortality, dictating the course of subsequent therapy [ ]. Extended pelvic lymph node dissection (ePLND) remains the gold standard for diagnosing LNM in PCa. However, significant variations exist across institutions in the sampling, sectioning, and evaluation strategies for ePLND specimens. Consensus remains lacking regarding optimal processing protocols and feasible quality control metrics. Routine histopathological assessment typically relies on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of limited tissue sections, which may fail to detect micrometastases with low tumor burden [ , ]. Clinically, it has also been observed that more than 20% of patients with pathologically node-negative disease (pN0) still experience postoperative tumor recurrence [ ]. Therefore, it is hypothesized that the recurrence may be attributable to the presence of clinically undetected micro-metastases within the lymph nodes. According to the 8th edition of the American Joint Cancer Committee (AJCC) Cancer Staging Manual, lymph node micro-metastases are defined as tumor deposits with a maximum diameter of 0.2 ~ 2.0mm [ ]. Studies demonstrate that PCR-based detection of LNM exhibits high sensitivity and specificity [ ]. This molecular approach serves as a valuable tool for guiding clinical decision-making and prognostic stratification in prostate cancer management [ ]. Currently, prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) are specific serum markers derived from prostate epithelial cells [ , ], which have important clinical significance in the diagnosis and treatment of PCa. Prostate cancer antigen 3 (PCA3) is a long non-coding RNA that is specifically overexpressed in prostate cancer cells and has been identified as one of the most prominent urinary biomarkers for the disease’s detection. Researches have shown that these three genes can be detected in metastatic PCa lymph nodes [ – ]. The genes encoding PSA and PSMA are Kallikrein-3 (KLK3) and Folate Hydrolase-1 (FOLH1), respectively. Addressing the current limitations in lymph node assessment for prostate cancer, this study innovatively quantifies the mRNA expression levels of KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 simultaneously in lymph node specimens. By systematically comparing the expression profiles of these molecular markers across lymph nodes with different pathological characteristics, patients were stratified into three subgroups based on combined histopathological and molecular status: pathology-negative/molecular-negative (pN0molN0), pathology-negative/molecular-positive (pN0molN1), and pathology-positive/molecular-positive (pN1molN1). The correlations between these classifications and postoperative BCR were analyzed to establish a reproducible lymph node “molecular staging” system and refined risk stratification strategy for PCa patients following RP, thereby providing molecular evidence for precise identification of high-risk populations and optimization of clinical decision-making. Materials and methods Patients selection Between April 2021 and August 2022, 26 prostate cancer patients who underwent RP combined with pelvic lymph node dissection (PLND) and 7 bladder cancer patients who underwent radical cystectomy (RC) combined with PLND (serving as controls) were enrolled in this study at Beijing Chaoyang Hospital, Capital Medical University. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Beijing Chaoyang Hospital. All resected lymph nodes underwent histopathological examination by two independent pathologists to determine the presence of LNM. Gleason grade was based on the 2014 International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) consensus, and clinical stage followed the 8th edition AJCC TNM staging system. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Age between 50 and 85 years; (2) Diagnosis of PCa and receipt of laparoscopic RP combined with PLND; (3) Clinical stage T2-T3 disease, suitable for surgery and without distant metastasis; (4) Ability to comply with postoperative follow-up. Patients with other systemic malignancies, severe comorbidities, or incomplete clinical data were excluded. Patients who received endocrine therapy (androgen deprivation therapy) after RP were excluded from the study. Neoadjuvant therapy consisted of combined androgen blockade (CAB) with abiraterone acetate plus leuprorelin for approximately 3 months, with an interval of approximately 2 weeks between the last dose and RP. Specimen collection and processing Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue sections were retrieved from the Department of Pathology, Beijing Chaoyang Hospital. The specimens originated from patients who underwent laparoscopic RP with PLND performed by a consistent surgical team between April 2021 and August 2022. Two experienced pathologists reviewed lymph node sections and selected 60 representative slides, encompassing both metastatic and non-metastatic lymph nodes from PCa patients. Among the 60 lymph nodes, one sample was excluded due to poor quality, making it unsuitable for PCR analysis. The corresponding paraffin block numbers for these slides were documented. from patients who underwent laparoscopic RP with PLND performed by a consistent surgical team between April 2021 and August 2022. Two experienced pathologists reviewed lymph node sections and selected 60 representative slides, encompassing both metastatic and non-metastatic lymph nodes from PCa patients. Among the 60 lymph nodes, one sample was excluded due to poor quality, making it unsuitable for PCR analysis. The corresponding paraffin block numbers for these slides were documented. For the control group, FFPE sections were also obtained from patients who underwent RC with PLND for bladder cancer during the same period. Pathologists confirmed the absence of prostate cancer cells in these control lymph nodes, and 11 qualifying slides were selected, with their corresponding tissue block numbers recorded. The cohort comprised 26 PCa patients and 7 bladder cancer patients. Among the prostate cancer patients, 10 cases were pathologically confirmed to have lymph node metastasis (pN1), with a total of 10 positive lymph nodes and 17 negative lymph nodes identified; 16 cases were negative for lymph node metastasis (pN0), with a total of 32 negative lymph nodes identified. For each selected paraffin block, ten consecutive 10 μm sections were cut using a microtome equipped with a new, disposable blade for each block to prevent cross-contamination. All sections were collected into sterile 1.5 mL tubes. Following collection, the tubes were stored at 4 °C, and the microtome was thoroughly cleaned after the entire sectioning procedure. RNA extraction RNA was extracted from paraffin-embedded sections. Briefly, tissues were deparaffinized with xylene, rehydrated through graded ethanol washes, and then digested with proteinase K in a lysis buffer at 55 °C for 8–12 h. Following proteinase K inactivation at 95 °C, total RNA was isolated from the supernatant using TRIzol reagent and chloroform and then precipitated with isopropanol. The RNA pellet was washed with 75% ethanol, air-dried, and finally dissolved in nuclease-free water. RNA concentration and purity were determined using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. Only samples with a concentration of > 200 ng/µL and an A260/A280 ratio between 1.8 and 2.0 were deemed qualified for subsequent analysis. cDNA synthesis and PCR RNA samples were thawed on ice, and reverse transcription reagents(TIANGEN) were incubated at room temperature. The RNA was mixed with a gDNA removal buffer and incubated at 42 °C for 3 min. A reverse transcription reaction mix was prepared and added to the RNA mixture, which was then incubated at 42 °C for 15 min, followed by 95 °C for 3 min. The resulting cDNA was stored at −20 °C. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was performed using commercial reagents (TIANGEN) on ice. The reaction mixture contained the qPCR master mix, specific primers (sequences listed in Table ), cDNA, ROX dye, and nuclease-free water. The thermal cycling protocol consisted of an initial denaturation at 95 °C for 15 min, followed by 40 cycles of 95 °C for 10 s, 60 °C for 20 s, and 72 °C for 32 s, with fluorescence acquisition during the extension step. A melting curve analysis was also performed at the end of the PCR cycles. For data analysis, a cycle threshold (Ct) value greater than 35 was defined as no expression. For samples with Ct ≤ 35, the relative expression levels of the KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 genes were calculated using the 2 –∆∆Ct method, with pelvic lymph nodes from male bladder cancer patients serving as the control group to establish a physiological baseline. Study endpoints and follow-up The primary endpoint of this study was biochemical recurrence-free survival (BRFS), defined as the time from RP to BCR. Postoperative monitoring involved serum PSA testing every three months for the first year, and every six months thereafter if no BCR occurred. BCR was defined as PSA exceeding 0.2 ng/mL twice consecutively after RP but without visible recurrent or metastatic lesions on imaging examination. In contrast, PSA persistence was defined as the failure of the postoperative PSA level to fall below 0.1 ng/mL within 4–6 weeks after RP date [ ], the event date for time-to-event analysis was defined as the date of surgery. The follow-up period was 2 years. Lymph node status was determined through pathological examination (designated pN1 if positive) and molecular analysis (designated molN1 if positive, based on elevated expression of one or more target genes). Subsequently, patients and lymph nodes were classified into one of four metastasis categories based on combined findings: pN1/molN1, pN1/molN0, pN0/molN1, and pN0/molN0. Continuous variables following a normal distribution were presented as mean ± standard deviation ( ±SD), whereas non-normally distributed data were expressed as median. Categorical data were summarized as frequencies (n). The four levels of LNM were considered ordinal variable. Statistical methods Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8 and R 4.2.3 software. Continuous variables following a normal distribution were presented as mean ± standard deviation ( ±SD), whereas non-normally distributed data were expressed as median. Categorical data were summarized as frequencies (n). The four levels of LNM were considered ordinal variable. Paired sample t-test was used to compare gene expression between positive and negative lymph nodes in PCa patients with LNM. An independent sample test was employed to compare gene expression levels between different groups of lymph nodes. Spearman correlation test was used to assess the correlation between lymph node metastasis levels in patients. BRFS was visualized using Kaplan–Meier curves for patients stratified by lymph node metastasis status (pN0molN0, pN0molN1, and pN1molN1). Risk factors of BRFS were identified through Cox regression analysis. p < 0.05 was considered a statistically significant difference. Results Clinical and pathological characteristics A total of 26 patients who underwent laparoscopic RP were enrolled in this study, comprising 10 with (pN1) and 16 without (pN0) pathologically confirmed LNM (Table ). The Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) nomogram was used to predict the risk of LNM. No significant differences were observed in PSA (pN1: 33.60 ± 27.06 vs. pN0: 25.30 ± 40.45 ng/mL), MSKCC-predicted risk (pN1: 54.10 ± 20.74% vs. pN0: 46.69 ± 22.48%), or positive biopsy core percentage (pN1: 59.10 ± 23.40% vs. pN0: 51.25 ± 26.20%). It is noteworthy that the pN1 group demonstrated numerically higher values among these parameters. Regarding treatment, 8 patients received neoadjuvant endocrine therapy. Pathological results of lymph nodes Figure outlines the study workflow. Our cohort consisted of 59 pelvic lymph nodes from 26 PCa patients and 11 nodes from 7 bladder cancer patients as controls. Based on the results, PCa patients and nodes were stratified into three groups: pN1molN1 (10 patients, 10 nodes), pN0molN1 (12 patients, 27 nodes), and pN0molN0 (4 patients, 22 nodes). Expression differences of KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 in lymph nodes of bladder cancer and PCa patients The expression of prostate-specific genes (KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3) was evaluated in 59 lymph nodes from PCa patients, with 10 lymph nodes from bladder cancer patients (without prostate disease history) serving as negative control tissues. As shown in Fig. , all three genes were significantly upregulated in PCa lymph nodes compared to control group (KLK3: p = 0.04; FOLH1: p = 0.005; PCA3: p = 0.01). The mean expression levels in the control group (KLK3: 0.41; FOLH1: 0.56; PCA3: 0.52) were established as physiological benchmarks. A lymph node was deemed molecularly positive (molN1) if the expression of any target gene exceeded its respective benchmark. Expression differences in all positive and negative lymph nodes To evaluate the expression differences of KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 in 10 pathologically positive lymph nodes and 49 negative lymph nodes, we performed an independent samples t-test. Consistent with Fig. , the expression levels of all three genes were significantly elevated in metastasis-positive lymph nodes compared with metastasis-negative nodes (KLK3: p = 0.0006; FOLH1: p = 0.01; PCA3: p = 0.04). Gene expression differences in metastatic and non-metastatic lymph nodes of PCa patients To evaluate differential gene expression within patients, we analyzed matched metastatic and non-metastatic lymph nodes from men with node-positive PCa (Fig. ). 10 positive lymph nodes and 17 negative lymph nodes were analyzed. Paired-sample t-test revealed that FOLH1 was significantly overexpressed in positive lymph nodes ( p = 0.02), while no significant differences were observed in the expression of KLK3 and PCA3 between the two groups. However, the expression levels of all three genes were higher in pN1 compared to pN0 within the same patient. Gene expression in negative lymph nodes from metastatic and non-metastatic patients Compared with 17 histologically negative lymph nodes from pN1 patients, the expression levels of KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 in 32 histologically negative lymph nodes from pN0 patients showed no statistically significant differences (Fig. ; p = 0.65, p = 0.97, and p = 0.56, respectively). Correlation between LNM levels and clinicopathological factors The extent of LNM was categorized as an ordinal variable (pN0molN0, pN0molN1, pN1molN1) for correlation analysis with clinicopathological factors. Spearman correlation analysis was employed to assess these associations (Table ). No statistically significant correlations were identified between the LNM level and any of the assessed variables, including age, preoperative PSA, ISUP grade, positive biopsy core percentage, clinical stage, MSKCC risk score, PSA, or neoadjuvant therapy ( p > 0.05). Postoperative BCR in PCa patients During a median follow-up of 13 months, BCR events were recorded (Table ). The median BRFS was 12 months. BCR rates were 30.0% (3/10) in patients with pathological node-positive (pN1) disease and 12.5%

No statistically significant correlations were identified between the LNM level and any of the assessed variables, including age, preoperative PSA, ISUP grade, positive biopsy core percentage, clinical stage, MSKCC risk score, PSA, or neoadjuvant therapy ( p > 0.05). Postoperative BCR in PCa patients During a median follow-up of 13 months, BCR events were recorded (Table ). The median BRFS was 12 months. BCR rates were 30.0% (3/10) in patients with pathological node-positive (pN1) disease and 12.5% (2/16) in pN0 patients. Based on molecular analysis, 21 patients had molecularly positive lymph nodes, and 5 experienced BCR, whereas no recurrences were observed in the molN0 group. Diagnostic value of KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 molecular analysis for BCR Using BCR as the standard, the sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) of the KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 genes were compared individually and in combination with pathological diagnosis (Table ). Among the individual markers, FOLH1 demonstrated the highest sensitivity (80.00%), while KLK3 exhibited the highest specificity (52.38%) and the highest PPV (23.08%) and NPV (84.62%). When the three genes were combined, sensitivity and NPV increased to 100%, though specificity decreased to 23.81%. In contrast, pathological diagnosis yielded a sensitivity of 60.00% and a specificity of 66.67%. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) was 0.81 for molecular pathological detection (Total) and 0.60 for histopathological detection (Fig. ). These results indicate that molecular analysis of lymph nodes enhances sensitivity and NPV for predicting BCR compared to pathological assessment alone. K-M survival curve of BRFS for PCa patients with different LNM levels Five patients experienced BCR (19.23%), with a median BRFS of 12 months. Among them, 3 patients had positive lymph nodes, and 2 had negative lymph nodes. Figure shows the Kaplan-Meier survival curves of patients with different levels of lymph node metastasis (pN0molN0, pN0molN1, pN1molN1) after pathological and molecular analysis. Patient information is provided in Supplementary 1. Clinically, patients in the pN1molN1 and pN0molN1 subgroups exhibited shorter BRFS compared to those in the pN0molN0 subgroup, but these differences did not reach statistical significance (pN0molN1 vs. pN0molN0, p = 0.19; pN1molN1 vs. pN0molN0, p = 0.14). K-M survival curves of BRFS for individual gene-based LNM Levels To further analyze the potential correlation between different molecular expressions in lymph nodes and BCR in patients, the three genes were grouped separately. Figure presents the Kaplan-Meier survival curves for LNM levels (pN0molN0, pN0molN1, pN1molN1, pN1molN0), as determined by KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 genes individually. For the KLK3 gene, the log-rank test p-values were 0.17 (pN0molN0 vs. pN0molN1), 0.58 (pN0molN0 vs. pN1molN1), and 0.054 (pN0molN0 vs. pN1molN0). The log-rank test p-values for comparisons between pN0molN0 vs. pN1molN1 and pN0molN0 vs. pN0molN1 were both 0.7, showing no significant statistical difference. Similarly, for the PCA3 gene, the log-rank test p-values were 0.22 (pN0molN0 vs. pN0molN1), 0.58 (pN0molN0 vs. pN1molN1), and 0.09 (pN0molN0 vs. pN1molN0). Notably, pN1molN0 patients in the KLK3 and PCA3 groups exhibited shorter BRFS. In contrast, these pN1molN0 patients (as defined by KLK3/PCA3) were reclassified as pN1molN1 when stratified by FOLH1 expression, suggesting discordant marker expression in pN1 patients—specifically, FOLH1 may remain positive while KLK3 and PCA3 are negative in the same lymph nodes. The biological and clinical implications of this heterogeneous molecular phenotype warrant further investigation. Discussion LNM detected during RP with ePLND constitutes a significant determinant of poor oncological outcomes in intermediate- and high-risk PCa [ , ]. Therefore, it is crucial to detect and remove any potential LNM. Clinical studies indicate that ePLND is associated with a higher detection rate of LNM [ ]. ePLND typically involves the removal of the obturator, internal iliac, external iliac, common iliac, and/or presacral lymph nodes. While histopathological examination of ePLND specimens is essential for accurate lymph node staging, there is no consensus on optimal specimen handling or universally accepted quality standards for identifying LNM. Standard histopathological methods may miss micrometastases due to sampling errors or oversight during microscopic review. Techniques such as graded sectioning and immunohistochemistry (IHC) can improve detection rates, but they are often time-consuming and costly [ , ]. Lymph node micrometastasis in PCa was first reported, which used PCR to identify two PSA mRNA–positive but histopathology-negative lymph nodes. [ ]. Although molecular assays cannot provide morphological details (e.g., lesion size or extracapsular extension), PCR-based methods may improve the detection of lymph node micrometastases beyond routine histopathology. Haas et al. further suggested combining H&E, IHC, and PCR on paraffin specimens to enable histology–molecular correlation; in 133 nodes from 68 patients, PCR for PSA yielded a PPV of 83% and an NPV of 100% versus pathology, though subsequent validation was limited. Although molecular assays cannot provide morphological details (e.g., lesion size or extracapsular extension), PCR-based methods may improve the detection of lymph node micrometastases beyond routine histopathology. Haas et al. further suggested combining H&E, IHC, and PCR on paraffin specimens to enable histology–molecular correlation; in 133 nodes from 68 patients, PCR for PSA yielded a PPV of 83% and an NPV of 100% versus pathology, though subsequent validation was limited. [ ]. Overall, PCR detection of PCa-specific markers (e.g., PSA, PSMA) can identify histopathology-negative but molecularly positive nodes (pN0molN1), and these expressions have been associated with postoperative BCR. [ , , ]. In clinical practice, multiple molecular markers are available for PCa. The KLK gene family, a subgroup of serine proteases, is often abnormally expressed in hormone-dependent tumors, particularly in the prostate. Among these, KLK3, which encodes PSA, has been favored by researchers. PSMA is also highly expressed in PCa and is associated with tumor invasiveness, making it a valuable marker for diagnosis and treatment, especially in positron emission tomography (PET) and single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) imaging [ ]. PCA3, a long non-coding RNA, is specifically expressed in about 95% of PCa cases and is upregulated 66-fold in tumors compared to normal prostate tissues. While KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 have been identified as potential molecular markers for lymph node analysis, their combined use in PCR detection has not been previously investigated. Given the significant genetic heterogeneity of PCa, the optimal markers for molecular lymph node analysis are yet to be determined. This study seeks to combine KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 as molecular markers for PCR-based detection of pelvic lymph nodes in prostate cancer. This study used paraffin-embedded lymph node specimens instead of fresh-frozen samples. Paraffin-embedded specimens directly confirm metastasis, aiding in clearer diagnoses while preserving lymph node integrity and preventing tumor lesions from being missed [ ]. However, RNA in these tissues degrades over time, leading to greater RNA loss. As a result, two lymph nodes were excluded due to low RNA concentrations, making them unsuitable for PCR testing. We compared the expression of prostate cancer-specific genes KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 in the lymph nodes of bladder cancer and PCa patients. The results showed significant upregulation of these genes in PCa patients’ lymph nodes. We also evaluated LNM by determining the relative expression threshold of these genes in the lymph nodes of bladder cancer patients. By comparing the gene expression levels of KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 in pathologically positive versus negative lymph nodes, we observed higher expression of these genes in metastatic lymph nodes. This suggests that molecular-level metastasis is more pronounced in metastatic lymph nodes compared to non-metastatic ones, consistent with previous studies [ , , , ]. We further compared gene expression profiles between metastatic and non-metastatic lymph nodes in PCa patients with pathologically confirmed nodal involvement. Elevated expression levels were observed in metastatic lymph nodes, consistent with a higher tumor burden and correspondingly increased molecular marker expression. However, only FOLH1 reached statistical significance, suggesting it may possess superior sensitivity compared to KLK3 and PCA3. The lack of significant differences for the latter two genes may be attributable to technical limitations such as RNA degradation or insufficient statistical power due to sample size constraints. In addition, we evaluated gene expression in histologically negative lymph nodes from pN1 and pN0 patients. Although not statistically significant, expression levels were consistently higher in negative lymph nodes from pN1 patients. Notably, these levels also exceeded those observed in lymph nodes from bladder cancer patients, raising the possibility of molecular micrometastases in histologically negative nodes from prostate cancer patients. Whether KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 expression levels in negative lymph nodes differ meaningfully across patient subgroups warrants further investigation in larger cohorts. In this study, LNM level showed consistent but non-significant positive trends with multiple clinical variables, including PSA, ISUP grade, and clinical stage. Previous studies have reported significant correlations with similar parameters [ ]; the discrepancy in our findings may stem from the small sample size and limited follow-up, underscoring the need for larger validation studies. Analysis of patients’ BCR showed that the higher the LNM level, the greater the proportion of patients with BCR (0% for pN0molN0, 18.18% for pN0molN1, and 30% for pN1molN1). The K-M survival curves for BRFS revealed that patients without LNM had the most favorable outcomes compared to established clinicopathological risk factors. Patients with molecularly positive lymph nodes showed intermediate outcomes, while those with both pathologically and molecularly positive lymph nodes had the worst outcomes. The FOLH1 K-M curve indicated a lower BCR risk in pN0molN0 patients, though not statistically significant. In contrast, pN1molN0 patients in the KLK3 and PCA3 groups showed higher recurrence risks, suggesting single-gene

the higher the LNM level, the greater the proportion of patients with BCR (0% for pN0molN0, 18.18% for pN0molN1, and 30% for pN1molN1). The K-M survival curves for BRFS revealed that patients without LNM had the most favorable outcomes compared to established clinicopathological risk factors. Patients with molecularly positive lymph nodes showed intermediate outcomes, while those with both pathologically and molecularly positive lymph nodes had the worst outcomes. The FOLH1 K-M curve indicated a lower BCR risk in pN0molN0 patients, though not statistically significant. In contrast, pN1molN0 patients in the KLK3 and PCA3 groups showed higher recurrence risks, suggesting single-gene molecular analysis may miss micrometastatic lymph nodes. This highlights the value of FOLH1 in enhancing detection, and combined PCR analysis of multiple genes improves sensitivity and reliability. As adjuvant therapy gains importance for lymph node-positive PCa after RP, optimizing LNM staging methods becomes critical. In addition to ePLND, molecular lymph node analysis serves as a valuable prognostic tool to guide further therapy. A randomized trial first showed that adjuvant endocrine therapy improved progression-free survival, overall survival, and disease-specific survival in prostate cancer patients post-surgery [ ]. Later studies confirmed that adjuvant androgen deprivation therapy improves survival in lymph node-positive PCa patients [ ]. For patients with molecularly positive lymph nodes, despite negative pathological results, adjuvant endocrine therapy should be considered. The identification of specific biomarkers for molecular detection of PCa in lymph nodes remains an active area of investigation. In a 2020 study by Heck et al. [ ],PCR analysis of six genes (KLK2, KLK3, KLK4, PSMA, TMPRSS2, and TRPM8) was performed in 111 patients. Using histopathology as the reference standard, KLK3 demonstrated the highest concordance (96%), followed by KLK2 (90%), TMPRSS2 (83%), KLK4 (81%), PSMA (77%), and TRPM8 (81%). Notably, KLK3 and TMPRSS2 positivity were statistically significant predictors of BRFS (HR = 6.8, 95% CI: 3.4–13.5). Additionally, KLK14 has been implicated in tumor metastasis [ ]. In a complementary study, Özdemir et al. [ ] reported elevated expression of epithelial markers—including PSA, PSCA, EpCAM, PSMA, NKX3-1, and AGR2—in lymph nodes of PCa patients, whereas markers related to stem cell characteristics, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and reactive stroma were not detected. Using BCR as the reference standard, the FOLH1 molecular marker demonstrated higher sensitivity than KLK3 and PCA3. The combined analysis of all three genes increased sensitivity to 100%, significantly surpassing the 60% sensitivity observed with pathological diagnosis. This finding suggests that molecular lymph node analysis can enhance the sensitivity of predicting BCR in PCa patients, corroborating previous studies [ , ]. This also suggests that combining different molecular markers can better predict postoperative BCR in PCa patients since not all markers are co-expressed. However, due to the low prevalence, these observations are preliminary and warrant further validation in larger patient cohorts. The neoadjuvant endocrine therapy employed in this study comprised an intensified androgen axis suppression regimen consisting of abiraterone acetate (typically co-administered with prednisone) combined with leuprorelin. Prior randomized phase II neoadjuvant trials have demonstrated that this regimen achieves deeper suppression of intratumoral androgens and reduces residual tumor burden/volume compared with LHRH agonist monotherapy, suggesting a potential mechanism for improving postoperative recurrence risk by diminishing local residual disease and putative micrometastatic “seeds" [ , ]. However, existing evidence predominantly reflects pathological improvements rather than unequivocal long-term biochemical benefit: in neoadjuvant trials such as ACDC-RP, patients achieving pathological complete response (pCR) or minimal residual disease (MRD) exhibited superior early-term (e.g., 12-month) BRFS, implying that “deeper pathological response” may correlate with reduced BCR risk. Nevertheless, definitive long-term BCR benefit at the population level awaits validation with more mature follow-up data [ ]. Our study utilized paraffin-embedded specimens, which led to some RNA degradation and consequently limited the robustness of our findings. However, with the continuous advancement of molecular biotechnology, one-step nucleic acid amplification (OSNA) technology can be employed for intraoperative molecular analysis of lymph nodes, minimizing RNA loss. Cytokeratin 19, a cytoplasmic intermediate filament protein, is specifically upregulated in tumor cells [ ]. Intraoperative frozen pathology using OSNA to detect cytokeratin 19 mRNA as a marker for lymph node metastasis has proven feasible [ ]. This highlights the potential of molecular lymph node analysis as a critical tool for PCa staging and for guiding ePLND during surgery. In recent years, the mechanisms of molecular LNM have also been continuously explored. Besides research on lymphangiogenic factors, EMT, and immune evasion [ – ], in 2021, Ren’s team [ ] performed single-cell sequencing on 13 patients and found that KLK3 was specifically expressed in a regulatory T cell subpopulation and two effector T cell subpopulations. for guiding ePLND during surgery. In recent years, the mechanisms of molecular LNM have also been continuously explored. Besides research on lymphangiogenic factors, EMT, and immune evasion [ – ], in 2021, Ren’s team [ ] performed single-cell sequencing on 13 patients and found that KLK3 was specifically expressed in a regulatory T cell subpopulation and two effector T cell subpopulations. The extracellular vesicle and exosome pathways were activated in the latter, suggesting that vesicles secreted by tumors mediate the transfer of KLK3 to T cells, indicating that molecular markers such as KLK3 may enter lymph nodes through exosomes secreted by tumor cells. This theory can be validated in future studies. This study has several limitations: (1) The small sample size may lead to selection bias. (2) The retrospective design limits the reliability and generalizability of the results. (3) RNA degradation in paraffin-embedded specimens may affect the outcomes. (4) Not all lymph nodes were dissected, potentially omitting samples. (5) The follow-up period was insufficient. Conclusion The molecular markers KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 show significantly higher expression in the pelvic lymph nodes of PCa patients. PCR-based analysis of these genes enables the molecular detection of lymph-node metastasis and, when combined with standard histopathological examination, improves the accuracy and sensitivity of lymph-node staging. Furthermore, it has potential utility in prognostic risk stratification for postoperative BCR. Therefore, molecular lymph-node assessment based on KLK3, FOLH1, and PCA3 may serve as a useful prognostic tool to guide adjuvant treatment decisions, although larger prospective studies are warranted to validate these findings.
